module_title: Periodic Trends: Radii, Ionization, and Electron Gain Enthalpies (Intermediate)
introduction: This intermediate tier drives into the core periodic properties and their variations across periods and groups. It heavily emphasizes the critical exceptions (due to half-filled/fully-filled stability and shielding) that are the primary focus of competitive exam questions.

core_concepts.title: Atomic and Ionic Radii
core_concepts.description:
Atomic radius generally DECREASES across a period (left to right) due to increasing effective nuclear charge pulling electrons closer. It INCREASES down a group due to the addition of new electron shells. 
Ionic Radii: Cations are always smaller than their parent atoms (loss of shell/increased $Z_{\text{eff}}$). Anions are always larger than their parent atoms (increased inter-electronic repulsion).

core_concepts.title: Isoelectronic Species
core_concepts.description: Atoms and ions containing the exact same number of electrons (e.g., $N^{3-}, O^{2-}, F^-, Ne, Na^+, Mg^{2+}, Al^{3+}$ all have 10 electrons). In an isoelectronic series, the size is INVERSELY proportional to the atomic number ($Z$). The species with the most protons ($Al^{3+}$, $Z=13$) exerts the strongest pull and is the smallest. The species with the fewest protons ($N^{3-}$, $Z=7$) is the largest.

core_concepts.title: Ionization Enthalpy ($\Delta_i H$)
core_concepts.description: The minimum energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom. It generally INCREASES across a period (due to decreasing size and increasing $Z_{\text{eff}}$) and DECREASES down a group. Successive ionization enthalpies always increase ($IE_3 > IE_2 > IE_1$) because it is harder to remove an electron from a progressively more positive ion.

core_concepts.title: Electron Gain Enthalpy ($\Delta_{eg} H$)
core_concepts.description:
The enthalpy change when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom to form a negative ion. It becomes more NEGATIVE (more energy released) across a period and less negative down a group. 
Important Note: While the FIRST electron gain enthalpy for most non-metals is negative (exothermic), the SECOND electron gain enthalpy (e.g., $O^- + e^- \rightarrow O^{2-}$) is ALWAYS POSITIVE (endothermic) due to electrostatic repulsion between the negative ion and the incoming electron.

core_concepts.title: Electronegativity (EN)
core_concepts.description: The qualitative ability of an atom in a chemical compound to attract shared electrons to itself. Pauling scale is widely used (Fluorine = 4.0, highest). EN INCREASES across a period and DECREASES down a group. Unlike IE and EGE, electronegativity is not a measurable energy value; it is a relative scale.

important_entities.name: First Ionization Enthalpy Anomalies
important_entities.significance: Be ($1s^2 2s^2$) has a higher $IE_1$ than B ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^1$) because removing a penetrating $s$-electron requires more energy than removing a $p$-electron. Similarly, N ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$) has a higher $IE_1$ than O ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$) because the half-filled $p^3$ configuration in Nitrogen confers extra stability.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: Electron Gain Enthalpy of F vs. Cl
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A classic JEE/NEET trap. One might expect Fluorine (F) to have the most negative electron gain enthalpy. However, Chlorine (Cl) has a MORE negative $\Delta_{eg} H$ than Fluorine. Reason: The fluorine atom is extremely small, resulting in high inter-electronic repulsions in its compact $2p$ subshell. The incoming electron experiences less repulsion in the larger $3p$ subshell of Chlorine.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Memorize the order of the most electronegative elements: F (4.0) > O (3.5) > N $\approx$ Cl (3.0) > Br (2.8) > I $\approx$ S $\approx$ C (2.5) > H (2.1). This helps instantly solve dipole moment and oxidation state polarity questions in organic and inorganic chemistry.

exam_strategy_tips: When comparing the 2nd Ionization Energy ($IE_2$), write out the configuration AFTER removing one electron. For example, $IE_1$ of O > $IE_1$ of F is FALSE. But for $IE_2$, O becomes $O^+$ (with a stable half-filled $2p^3$ configuration) and F becomes $F^+$ ($2p^4$). Therefore, $IE_2$ of O is vastly GREATER than $IE_2$ of F.
